chapters.name: Sign Shapes, Colors, and Regulatory Signs
chapters.summary: What sign shapes and colors mean, and the white, black, and red signs that state rules you must obey.
keyPoints: The red eight-sided sign always means stop. The red and white triangle pointing down means yield.
White rectangle signs with black or red letters state rules, such as speed limits, ONE WAY, and no turns.
Red is used for stop, yield, DO NOT ENTER, and WRONG WAY. Green guides you, blue shows services, and brown leads to parks and recreation.

chapters.name: Warning, School, and Work Zone Signs
chapters.summary: Yellow diamond warning signs, school and pedestrian signs, railroad warning signs, and orange work zone signs.
keyPoints: Yellow diamond signs warn of a hazard or change in the road ahead, such as a crossroad, a stop sign ahead, or two-way traffic.
The five-sided sign marks a school zone or school crossing. Fluorescent yellow-green is used for school, pedestrian, and bicycle warnings.
The round yellow sign warns of a railroad crossing ahead. Orange signs mark work zones.

chapters.name: Traffic Signals and Pavement Markings
chapters.summary: How to respond to steady and flashing lights, arrows, and dark signals, and what yellow and white lines on the road tell you.
keyPoints: A flashing red light means stop, then go as if at a stop sign. A flashing yellow light means go with caution.
If a signal shows no lights at all, stop and yield as you would at a stop sign.
Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes going the same way.

chapters.name: Right of Way, School Buses, and Emergency Vehicles
chapters.summary: Who goes first at intersections, stop and yield signs, and driveways, and how to act around pedestrians, school buses, and emergency vehicles.
keyPoints: When two vehicles reach an intersection at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
Stop at least 10 feet from a school bus that is stopped to load or unload children. On a road with four or more lanes, traffic coming from the other direction does not have to stop.
Pull over to the right and stop for an emergency vehicle using its lights and siren. Move over or slow down for stopped vehicles with flashing lights.

chapters.name: Speed, Passing, and Parking
chapters.summary: Ohio speed limits, the assured clear distance rule, safe passing, and the places where you may not park.
keyPoints: Unless posted otherwise, the limit is 20 mph in a school zone during school hours, 25 mph in most of a city or village, and 55 mph on highways outside cities and villages.
When passing on a two-lane road, return to your lane before you come within 200 feet of an oncoming vehicle.
Do not park within 10 feet of a fire hydrant, 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, 30 feet of a stop sign, yield sign, or traffic signal, or 50 feet of a railroad crossing.

chapters.name: Safe Driving Practices
chapters.summary: Headlights, turn signals, following distance, lanes and turns, seat belts and child seats, phones, and railroad crossings.
keyPoints: Turn on headlights from sunset to sunrise, when you cannot see 1,000 feet ahead, and when you use wipers because of rain or snow.
Signal continuously for at least the last 100 feet before you turn or change lanes.
When railroad signals flash or a gate is down, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail.

chapters.name: Temporary Permit (TIPIC) and Probationary License
chapters.summary: Who can get a temporary instruction permit, who must ride with a permit holder, and the rules for young drivers with a probationary license.
keyPoints: You can apply for a temporary instruction permit at 15 years and 6 months. The permit is valid for one year.
Drivers under 18 must hold the permit at least 6 months and complete 50 hours of driving, including 10 at night.
Permit holders under 18 may not drive from midnight to 6 a.m. unless a parent, guardian, or custodian rides beside them.

chapters.name: OVI: Alcohol and Drug Laws
chapters.summary: Ohio's alcohol limits for adults and drivers under 21, the implied consent law, and the penalties for operating a vehicle impaired (OVI).
keyPoints: A driver with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08% or more is violating Ohio's OVI law.
A driver under 21 violates the law at 0.02% or more.
Refusing a chemical test for the first time brings a one-year administrative license suspension. Failing a test for the first time brings a three-month suspension.
